metas.name: Aguascalientes - Aguascalientes
metas.note: This plate features a thin orange stripe along the top and another along the bottom, making it relatively straightforward to identify among Mexican state plates. The center of the plate is white, with a faint round symbol visible in the background. Note that this is an older plate design, so you will mostly encounter it in older Street View coverage. The vast majority of plates from this state are generation 3.

metas.note: This plate is characterized by a blue stripe at the top and a light-blue center. The bottom typically displays a green stripe. In short, the overall color scheme is blue and green. Occasionally, a distinct dot is visible on the left side of the plate.

metas.name: Baja California Orange - Baja California Orange Green

metas.name: Baja california red - Baja california red

metas.name: Campeche - Campeche
metas.note: This plate features a multicolored stripe along the bottom, displaying a alternating array of colors. When the plate is unblurred, the stripe reveals a distinctive cityscape motif made up of small houses in various colors. It can be tricky to identify at a glance, but a good rule of thumb is: if you spot a white plate with a heavily multicolored bottom stripe, it is very likely from Campeche.

metas.name: Chiapas - Chiapas
metas.note: This plate is white with a distinctive colored corner on each of its four corners: yellow or orange on the upper left, green on the upper right, red on the lower left, and blue on the lower right. This four-color corner pattern makes it one of the most unique and easily recognizable plates among all Mexican states.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Chihuaha blue - Chihuaha blue
metas.note: This plate is predominantly white, with a thick blue stripe running along the bottom. The blue band is centered at the lower portion of the plate and is quite clearly visible even from a distance. The rest of the plate is plain white with no other notable color elements.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Chihuaha red - Chihuaha red
metas.note: This plate features a thick red stripe along the top, paired with a much thinner red line along the bottom. The contrast between the bold upper stripe and the subtle lower line is a useful detail to keep in mind when identifying this plate.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Coahuila black line - Coahuila black line
metas.note: This is a relatively recent plate design, introduced in 2022, and is characterized by a thick black stripe along the bottom. It is commonly encountered in the newer Street View coverage of Coahuila.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Colima brown - Colima brown green
metas.note: This is an older Colima plate design, but it appears frequently in the older Street View coverage of the state. The plate features a brown stripe on the bottom left and a green stripe on the bottom right. When the plate is blurred, these two stripes appear as a brown triangle and a green triangle, which can still serve as a useful identifying clue even at low resolution.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Colima mexican flag - Colima mexican flag
metas.note: This is arguably one of the most recognizable Mexican state plates. It features a stripe along the bottom divided into the three colors of the Mexican flag: green on the left, white in the middle, and red on the right. Even when the plate is blurred, this tricolor band remains clearly visible, making it exceptionally easy to identify at a glance.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Durango 23 - Durango new
metas.note: This is the newest Durango plate design, introduced in 2023, and is frequently found unblurred in Street View. Its most useful identifying feature is visible even when blurred: two orange dots, one on the bottom left and one on the bottom right of the plate. This plate is very common in the latest Street View coverage of Durango.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Durango green line - Durango Red and Green
metas.note: This is an older Durango plate design, most commonly encountered in older Street View coverage, though it occasionally appears unblurred in more recent imagery as well. When blurred, the key identifying features are a red background in the center and a green stripe along the bottom.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Durango yellow blue purple line - Durango yellow, blue and purple
metas.note: This white plate features a distinctive thin striped line along the bottom, made up of three colors in the following order: yellow, blue, and purple. Once you memorize this specific color sequence, the plate becomes very easy to identify. The combination is quite unique among Mexican state plates, making it one of the more memorable designs.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Guanajuato - Guanajuato old

metas.name: Guerrero new plate - Guerrero new plate

metas.name: Hidalgo red line - Hidalgo new plate
metas.note: This is the newest Hidalgo plate design, introduced in 2023. When blurred, its key identifying feature is a thick dark red stripe along the bottom, which can sometimes appear purple depending on the image quality. This plate is widespread throughout the newer Street View coverage of Hidalgo.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: jalisco new plate - Jalisco new plate
metas.note: Jalisco has two recent plate designs one from 2019 and one from 2023 which are very similar to each other. Both share the same key identifying feature: a small thick stripe along the top of an otherwise white plate. When blurred, this stripe can appear either dark blue or dark green depending on the image. If you spot a white plate with a narrow but prominent top stripe in one of these dark tones, Jalisco is a strong guess.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Jalisco old plate  - Jalisco old plate
metas.note: This is the older Jalisco plate design, predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of the state. It is one of the easier plates to recognize and remember, as it has a distinctly yellow top half and a blue bottom half, making it stand out clearly even in lower quality imagery.

metas.name: mexico state  - Estado de México
metas.note: This plate is predominantly found in the older Street View coverage of Estado de México but also can be seen in the new coverage. It has a bluish background with two red stripes: a thicker one along the top and a thinner one along the bottom. The combination of the blue background and dual red stripes makes it one of the easier plates to identify with confidence.

metas.name: Michoacan redline - Michoacán new

Its most distinctive feature is a very thick stripe along the top, which can appear either dark red or purple depending on image quality. This plate is widely encountered throughout the newer Street View coverage of Michoacán.

metas.name: morelos - Morelos
metas.note: Morelos has two recent plate designs one from 2019 and one from 2022 which are very similar to each other. When blurred, both appear as a white plate with a large red dot on the bottom right. Once you know to look for that red dot on the right side, this plate becomes quite easy to identify.

metas.name: Nayarit 22 - Nayarit new plate
metas.note: This is the newest Nayarit plate design, introduced in 2022. It features a fairly thick multicolored stripe along the bottom, which can be tricky to identify when blurred. The key is to memorize the color order: light orange on the left, followed by blue and red in the middle, and green on the right. Remembering that the green is always on the right and the light orange always on the left is the most reliable way to distinguish this plate from others.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: New Nayarit purple line  - Nayarit Purple line
metas.note: Nayarit has two older plate designs, both featuring a thin purple stripe along the bottom. The earliest version, released in 2016, includes a mountain scene in the background, and when blurred its purple stripe takes on an unusual triangular shape. The second version, released in 2017, is simpler, displaying just a plain thin purple line at the bottom with no background imagery. Both designs are predominantly found in Street View coverage from 2016 to 2020.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Nuevo Leon  - Nuevo Leon
metas.note: This plate is entirely white with no notable color elements, making it one of the plainest Mexican state plates. Even when blurred, faint black text remains visible in the center. Its stark, minimalist appearance makes it relatively straightforward to recognize once you are familiar with it.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Old Nayarit - Nayarit old plate

metas.name: old quintana roo  - Quintana Roo old plate

When blurred, it displays a multicolored stripe along the bottom in the following order: green and yellow on the left, a visible orange dot in the middle, and a yellowish or green tone on the right. This plate is frequently seen unblurred in Street View, making it one of the easier ones to identify with confidence.

As with the other old Veracruz design, this plate is frequently seen unblurred in Street View, making it straightforward to identify.

The plate is white with a thick purple or dark red stripe that begins roughly in the middle of the plate and extends to the right. This distinctive half-stripe design makes it quite easy to recognize once you know what to look for.

metas.name: San Luis Potosi - San Luis Potosi

Both designs are found across old and new Street View coverage of the state. The plate is white with a thick green stripe along the top, though notably the green does not extend all the way to the left edge, leaving a small white gap on the left side. This partial top stripe is the key detail to remember when identifying this plate.

metas.name: Sinaloa old plate - Sinaloa old plate
metas.note: In contrast to the newer design, this older Sinaloa plate is very easy to recognize. When blurred, a large red dot appears prominently in the center of the plate, giving it a striking resemblance to the Japanese flag. This design dates back to 2006 and was used until 2011, so it is only found in the oldest Street View coverage of Sinaloa.

metas.name: Sinaloa white - Sinaloa
metas.note: This is arguably the hardest Mexican state plate to identify. The plate is entirely white with only a very thin red stripe along the bottom. When blurred, it appears as an almost completely white plate with just a faint hint of red at the bottom edge. Even if the red is barely visible, that subtle touch of color at the bottom is enough to confidently identify it as a Sinaloa plate.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Sonora old plate  - Sonora old plate

The plate is white with a very thin purple stripe along the bottom and a large orange dot on the right side. The combination of purple at the bottom and a prominent orange dot is the key detail to remember if you spot both of these features together, it is definitively a Sonora plate.

Even when blurred, keeping that simple color order in mind blue left, green right is enough to identify this plate with confidence.
